job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a section-by-section list. I've marked each item as **[Loophole]** (a reading that could permit continued operations), **[Ambiguity]** (unclear text a court or agency would have to resolve), or **[Drafting defect]** (internal inconsistency, missing machinery, or unworkability). Several items could serve both purposes.

## Sec. 2(1) — Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — per-vessel threshold. [Loophole]** The 10,000-metric-ton threshold is measured "by a single vessel," not per operator, project, or contract area. An operator could run two or more production vessels each recovering under 10,000 tons, or rotate vessels, and never trigger the definition even at full commercial scale.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery . . . by a single vessel" doesn't match how nodule mining works. [Loophole / Ambiguity]** Nodules are lifted by a seabed collector and riser system, received by a production vessel, and transferred at sea to shuttle or bulk carriers. The text doesn't say which vessel "recovers," and the seabed collector itself is arguably not a "vessel," so there is a credible argument that no single vessel recovers anything from the seabed.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "per year" undefined. [Ambiguity]** Calendar year, fiscal year, rolling 12 months, or first-year-from-effective-date is unspecified. With the 180-day delayed effective date (Sec. 8), it's unclear whether tonnage recovered before the effective date counts toward the first year.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — tonnage basis undefined. [Ambiguity]** Nodules are roughly 30–40% water by weight as recovered. The bill doesn't say whether the 10,000 tons is wet or dry weight, in situ or as landed, so the effective threshold could differ by thousands of tons depending on the reading.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters" is overbroad. [Drafting defect]** Oil and gas are mineral resources, and deepwater production in the Gulf of Mexico recovers far more than 10,000 tons per year from beneath the seabed at depths over 200 meters. Unless "from the seabed" is read to exclude subsoil hydrocarbons (and nothing in the text says so), the bill as written arguably criminalizes deepwater oil and gas production, FPSO operations, and possibly offshore aggregate and phosphorite recovery. This is a strong "unworkable" argument.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery" undefined. [Ambiguity]** It's unclear whether recovery means detachment from the seabed, lifting through the water column, or landing on a vessel. This matters for threshold accounting, for who the violator is, and for whether test-mining and sampling count.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "the Secretary" is never defined. [Drafting defect]** The Act refers to the Secretary of State (Sec. 6) and to NOAA, which is in Commerce (Sec. 4), but subparagraph (B) just says "the Secretary." No official is identifiably authorized to make the determination, so (B) may be inoperative.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — criminal liability by administrative determination with no procedure. [Drafting defect / Vagueness]** The Secretary can expand the definition of a crime carrying 10 years' imprisonment by finding "comparable" risks, with no rulemaking, notice, publication, hearing, or judicial-review provision and no standard for "comparable." This invites void-for-vagueness and due process challenges, and raises nondelegation concerns in the criminal context.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — no temporal scope. [Ambiguity]** It's unclear whether a determination applies prospectively only, or whether an operator could be penalized for conduct that occurred before the determination was made.

## Sec. 2(2) — Definition of "U.S. person"

10. **Sec. 2(2) — "corporation" only. [Loophole]** LLCs, limited partnerships, LLPs, trusts, and other non-corporate entities are not "U.S. persons." A corporation could convert to an LLC under state law or conduct operations through a non-corporate affiliate and fall outside the extraterritorial prohibition.

11. **Sec. 2(2) — "organized under the laws of a State." [Loophole / Ambiguity]** "State" is undefined and the usual boilerplate including the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other territories is absent. Entities organized under D.C., territorial, or tribal law arguably aren't covered.

12. **Sec. 2(2) — foreign subsidiaries and controlled entities not covered. [Loophole]** There is no ownership, control, or "foreign branch" language. A U.S. corporation's foreign-organized subsidiary is not a U.S. person, and the Act doesn't prohibit a U.S. person from owning, financing, directing, or contracting with one.

13. **Sec. 2(2) — individuals. [Loophole / Ambiguity]** Only "citizens" are covered, so lawful permanent residents and other U.S.-resident non-citizens are outside the extraterritorial prohibition (though they're reached while physically "in the United States" under Sec. 3(a)).

## Sec. 2(3) — Definition of "covered vessel"

14. **Sec. 2(3) — "equipped for the recovery" is vague and the tonnage floor is arbitrary. [Ambiguity]** A vessel can be equipped for recovery in port and de-equipped at sea; a 4,900-GT vessel is never covered. "Covered vessel" also appears only in Sec. 4, so the definition does nothing for the prohibition itself.

## Sec. 3 — Prohibition

15. **Sec. 3(a) — "engage in" undefined; no secondary liability. [Loophole]** The Act doesn't reach financing, chartering, insuring, supplying, purchasing, processing, or transporting recovered nodules, and contains no aiding-and-abetting, conspiracy, or "cause to be" language. A U.S. person could own the ore, fund the operation, and process the product onshore without "engaging in" mining if the vessel is operated by a non-U.S. entity.

16. **Sec. 3(a) — "person in the United States" is unclear for conduct at sea. [Ambiguity]** Mining occurs offshore, so the question is whether a Houston-based company directing operations is "in the United States" engaging in mining. "United States" is also undefined, leaving open whether it includes the territorial sea, EEZ, or outer continental shelf.

17. **Sec. 3(a) — no vessel-flag hook. [Loophole]** Unlike most U.S. maritime statutes, the bill never applies to U.S.-flagged vessels. A foreign-flagged vessel operated by a foreign entity is entirely outside the Act even if U.S.-owned.

18. **Sec. 3(b) — grandfather clause is extremely broad. [Loophole]** Any "mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment" is exempt. The clause doesn't require that the license be U.S.-issued (an ISA exploration contract or a foreign-sponsored license arguably qualifies), doesn't limit the exemption to activities actually authorized by the license, and doesn't cap tonnage.

19. **Sec. 3(b) — no treatment of renewals, extensions, amendments, or transfers. [Loophole / Ambiguity]** A pre-enactment license that is later renewed, expanded in area, or assigned to another entity is still "issued before the date of enactment" on a plain reading. The exemption could persist indefinitely and could be bought and sold.

20. **Sec. 3(b) — "exploration license" vs. commercial recovery. [Ambiguity / Drafting defect]** Under DSHMRA, NOAA issues exploration licenses and separate commercial recovery permits. The bill grandfathers mining under exploration licenses but says nothing about pre-enactment commercial recovery permits, so the most clearly commercial authorization is unaddressed, while exploration licenses (which usually permit test mining) are expressly protected.

21. **Sec. 3(b) — enactment-date trigger creates a licensing window. [Loophole]** The exemption is keyed to enactment, not introduction or markup, so licenses or contracts issued between now and the President's signature qualify. Combined with Sec. 8, there is a further 180-day period after enactment during which the prohibition doesn't apply at all.

22. **Sec. 3(c) — environmental-assessment exemption is unbounded. [Loophole]** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, there is no tonnage cap, no agency approval requirement, no limit on sale of recovered material, and no requirement that assessment be the sole or primary purpose. A commercial-scale operation with an integrated environmental monitoring program has a plausible argument that it is conducted "for the purpose of environmental assessment."

## Sec. 4 — Registry

23. **Sec. 4 — no deadline, no rulemaking authority, no penalty. [Drafting defect]** Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3, so failure to register or report carries no sanction. NOAA is given no authority to issue rules, prescribe forms, or set a registration deadline.

24. **Sec. 4 — "operator" undefined; no jurisdictional limit. [Ambiguity]** It's unclear whether the owner, charterer, manager, or master must register, and the provision on its face purports to require registration of every covered vessel in the world regardless of flag or nationality.

25. **Sec. 4(b) — compelled self-reporting of criminal conduct. [Drafting defect]** Requiring a certified quarterly description of "recovery activities" when such activities are criminalized creates a Fifth Amendment problem for individual operators and may make the reporting requirement unenforceable against them. It also implicitly assumes recovery activities continue, which sits awkwardly with Sec. 3.

## Sec. 5 — Penalties

26. **Sec. 5(a) — penalty clock conflicts with effective date. [Drafting defect]** Civil penalties attach to violations "occurring on or after the date of enactment," but under Sec. 8 nothing is unlawful until 180 days later. Either the penalty language is surplus or it attempts to penalize conduct that was lawful when it occurred, which would be challenged as retroactive.

27. **Sec. 5(a) — daily penalty for an annual-threshold offense. [Ambiguity]** The offense is defined by tonnage "per year," so a violation can't be established until the threshold is crossed, yet the penalty is "for each day on which the violation occurs." It's unclear whether penalties run from the first day of recovery, the day the threshold is crossed, or only days after crossing.

28. **Sec. 5 — no enforcing agency, no procedure, no remedies. [Drafting defect]** No agency is authorized to assess or collect civil penalties, no administrative or judicial procedure is specified, and there is no provision for injunctive relief, seizure, forfeiture, boarding, or inspection. Enforcement would depend entirely on DOJ bringing an action under general authority with no statutory hook for interdiction at sea.

29. **Sec. 5(a) — strict liability civil penalty tied to Sec. 2(1)(B). [Drafting defect]** A person can incur up to $1 million per day for conduct that became "commercial deep seabed mining" only by an unpublished determination of an undefined Secretary, with no knowledge requirement.

## Sec. 6 — International agreement

30. **Sec. 6 — hortatory with no consequence. [Drafting defect]** "Seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to conclude an agreement, and the prohibition is not conditioned on one. The provision concedes that a unilateral U.S. prohibition is incomplete without foreign participation while doing nothing to secure it.

## Sec. 7 — Duration

31. **Sec. 7(a) and 7(b) are inconsistent. [Drafting defect]** Subsection (a) says the prohibition continues until Congress finds by joint resolution that mining can be done safely; subsection (b) says the entire Act expires after 10 years. The sunset controls on a plain reading, which makes the "until Congress finds" language meaningless after year 10.

32. **Sec. 7(a) — the lifting mechanism is illusory. [Drafting defect]** No one is directed or funded to commission the National Academies report, "serious harm" is undefined, and a joint resolution is ordinary legislation requiring presentment, which Congress could pass anyway. The provision adds nothing and arguably implies the prohibition can't be lifted without an NAS report even if Congress wants to lift it.

33. **Sec. 7(b) — sunset effect on pending enforcement is unclear. [Ambiguity]** "Cease to have effect" is not the same as "repealed," so it's uncertain whether the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. 109) preserves liability for pre-sunset violations or whether pending penalty actions abate when the Act expires.

## Sec. 8 — Effective date and general omissions

34. **Sec. 8 — 180-day gap. [Loophole / Drafting defect]** Nothing is prohibited for 180 days after enactment, during which operators can recover without limit, obtain licenses (see item 21), reorganize corporate structures (items 10–12), and reflag vessels (item 17).

35. **No conforming amendments to DSHMRA. [Drafting defect]** The Act neither amends nor repeals the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.), so NOAA remains statutorily authorized to issue exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits for the very activity this bill prohibits. Two federal statutes would point in opposite directions.

36. **No severability clause. [Drafting defect]** If Sec. 2(1)(B), Sec. 5(a), or the Sec. 7 duration provisions fall to a constitutional or vagueness challenge, there is no express direction to preserve the remainder.

37. **No definitions for "person," "vessel," "Secretary," "State," "United States," "operator," "recovery," or "environmental assessment." [Drafting defect]** Most of the ambiguities above trace to the absence of a standard definitions section; the Dictionary Act fills some gaps (e.g., "person" includes corporations) but not the ones that matter most here.

---

**Two practical notes for the legal team.** First, items flagged as loopholes are plain-text readings; a court applying a purposive reading, especially of Sec. 3(b)–(c), might narrow them, and the Sec. 5(b) criminal exposure means reliance on any of them should be assessed carefully rather than assumed. Second, the drafting-defect items (especially 5, 7–8, 26, 31, 35) are the strongest material for markup because they show the bill is unworkable as written regardless of one's view of the policy; the loophole items, if raised publicly, will likely be closed in the manager's package, so consider which ones you want to surface and which you'd rather hold.
